Reducing Disparity Between LLMs and Humans: Optimal LLM Sample Calibration

Yan Leng
University of Texas at Austin - McCombs School of Business

Yunxin Sang
University of Texas at Austin - McCombs School of Business

Ashish Agarwal
University of Texas at Austin - McCombs School of Business

https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=4802019

https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/mksc.2024.0983


Abstract:

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to measure preferences and opinions, but their responses can diverge from those of the human populations they are meant to represent. Analysts typically rely on a single aggregate prompt or combine multiple LLM outputs using heuristic rules, such as uniform averaging, population-weighted post-stratification, or selecting the best single subgroup on a calibration split. These approaches can remain misaligned with human benchmarks. We propose Human Mimicry Calibration (HuMCal), a post-hoc, model-agnostic method that learns how to combine LLM outputs from different prompts, personas, or model checkpoints. Our method uses aggregate human benchmark data but requires no access to model internals or separate human benchmarks for each subgroup. On the calibration data, HuMCal chooses the weighted average that best matches the human benchmark; solved exactly, its calibration loss is therefore weakly lower than that of any fixed-weight rule over the same set of outputs, including uniform weighting, post-stratification, and the best single subgroup. We evaluate HuMCal in a revealed-preference market-structure application using U.S. bank-card transactions and in a public-opinion application using Pew survey data. Across both settings, HuMCal improves agreement on the calibration split relative to all evaluated fixed-weight baselines. Out of sample, the learned weights outperform heuristic baselines in most evaluated transfers across time, geography, industry, and question clusters. In the market-structure application, recalibration with newer LLM checkpoints improves agreement in all evaluated settings. These results suggest that HuMCal can serve as a scalable calibration tool for LLM-based measurement when collecting fresh benchmark data for each target setting is costly.

Keywords: large language model, calibration, preference learning, opinion learning, data collection, LLM-based measurement, preference measurement, opinion measurement, synthetic respondents
